query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an optimized thermomechanical treatment consisting of controlled cold rolling followed by tailored low‐temperature annealing to the uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will induce beneficial phase decomposition, creating a refined duplex microstructure that significantly enhances its strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion tolerance under cyclic thermal and mechanical loads.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual fcc/B2 phase structure in its as-cast state.
generation.intervention: Optimized thermomechanical treatment—specifically, controlled cold rolling (e.g., an 8% thickness reduction) followed by a low-temperature annealing regime tailored to promote partial phase decomposition.
generation.conditions: Simulated service conditions including extreme temperature fluctuations (room temperature up to ~700°C), long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and exposure to corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure with distributed nanoscale precipitates formed through controlled phase decomposition within the lamellar fcc/B2 matrix.
generation.mechanism: The thermomechanical treatment introduces microstructural heterogeneity that increases dislocation barriers and activates self-generated microcrack arrest mechanisms, thereby simultaneously enhancing strength and ductility while improving resistance to creep and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit increased yield and fracture strengths, improved elongation, reduced creep rates at room temperature, and lower corrosion rates compared to its initial as-cast state.
generation.baseline: The starting alloy, which in its as-cast fine lamellar condition shows a fracture strength near 944 MPa (engineering) or 1186 MPa (true stress) and ~25% elongation, but falls short of industrial performance requirements for fasteners.
generation.boundary: Expected performance improvements are valid within the temperature range up to 700°C under laboratory-scale mechanical, creep, and corrosion testing conditions that mimic industrial fastener service environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of enhancements in creep resistance and corrosion behavior remains uncertain due to variability in phase decomposition kinetics and potential impurity effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one subjected to the optimized thermomechanical treatment (controlled cold rolling with an 8% reduction followed by low-temperature annealing) and a control group in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to standardized tensile, creep, and corrosion tests under simulated service conditions (including temperature cycling between room temperature and 700°C, sustained mechanical loading, and corrosive environments).
measurements: Creep rate (via nanoindentation or comparable method)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements (p < 0.05) in strength, ductility, reduced creep rate, and improved corrosion resistance compared to the as-cast control samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. reading.lever: Apply an optimized thermomechanical treatment (controlled cold rolling followed by tailored low-temperature annealing) to induce beneficial phase decomposition for enhanced strength, ductility, and creep resistance.
reading.why: This combined approach, evidenced in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 studies, directly addresses the alloy’s performance limits under extreme loading and corrosive, fluctuating temperatures by refining its microstructure.
